card.summary: What a frequency scout is for. The dark bands of balanced SSFP repeat every 1 / TR in frequency; where the marked regions fall in that pattern depends on the field, on the error of the frequency adjustment, on the material (oil sits 3.4 ppm below water) and on the repetition time, and how wide a band is depends on the material and on the excitation. The target is a 2D image: the slice profile of the selective pulse adds spins at smaller flip angles, whose signal peaks next to the band, so the band is narrower than the hard-pulse formula says and a band model has to carry the slice profile (a 3D acquisition with a hard pulse costs a multiple of the scan time and shows another band). A low bandwidth gives the least noise and the longest repetition time. The answer, for each of the two images, is the lowest bandwidth at which one phase cycle keeps every region clear of the bands with a margin for frequency drift, or the recognition that no single acquisition can, and then the pair of phase cycles that does. By level: level 1 is a measurement task, level 2 is a measurement task, level 3 is a measurement task (a fixed list of scans with a fixed estimator passes this many points below the reference: -2.3 at level 1, -1.3 at level 2, -1 at level 3; 300 instances per level; 25 points or more make a decision task).

A test object with vials of unknown materials lies in the field of
view. The examination needs two balanced SSFP images of it, image A and image B, each with a protocol of its own:
    sequence bssfp, flip_deg 60, matrix 120, field of view at the console default, slice 5 mm with the console's
    default slice-selective pulse, 1 average, bandwidth_hz_per_px of your choice between 60 and 600, tr_ms at the console
    minimum for that bandwidth (a plan shows it), phase_cycle_deg of your choice
No dark band may cross the marked regions of an image (circles; centre and radius in mm from the isocentre; each lies
inside one homogeneous material):
  image A
  R1: y 57.57, x 6.07, radius 6
  R2: y 12.91, x 56.44, radius 6
  R3: y -45.15, x 30.81, radius 6
  image B
  R4: y -39.18, x -34.86, radius 6
  R5: y 27.6, x -47.33, radius 6
Deliver with `submit`, for each image, the bandwidth and one phase cycle. If no single acquisition can keep every
marked region of an image out of the bands, deliver for that image the bandwidth and two phase cycles: two
acquisitions that differ only in the phase cycle. Every region is then read from one of the two, the one that shows

   frequency and at every drift of the centre frequency of up to 20 Hz either way (the same drift everywhere in the
   object).

   less is band-free for that image.

   most 1.15 times the lowest bandwidth at which a band-free protocol with the same number of acquisitions exists
   for that image.

that only just exists does not count against you.

0.hints:
How to do it (this level states the procedure).
  1. Probe with `ir` at a repetition time short enough for several scans (for example tr_ms 800, matrix 64,
     partial_fourier 0.6, bandwidth_hz_per_px 300): three or more inversion times spread from 60 ms to
     tr_ms - 50 ms, read out on the marked regions.
  2. Sign the signal. At the longest inversion time every material is past its null, so its signal is positive. A
     read-out whose phase differs from the region's phase in that scan by more than pi / 2 is negative.
  3. Per region, fit S(TI) = a - b exp(-TI / T1) to the signed signals. Let q = b / a.
  4. The probes ran at another repetition time than the target scan, so carry the fit over. With E(TR) = exp(-(TR - TE / 2) / T1):
     k = (q - 1) / (1 - q E(TR_probe)), then TI_null = T1 ln((1 + k) / (1 + k E(TR_target))).
